topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Sometimes the useful abstraction is a result that will become available, not a thread that must be managed directly. Futures and promises provide a one-result communication channel, while async can arrange execution under a selected policy. This chapter transfers both a value and an exception, distinguishes deferred work from asynchronous work, and explains why a future’s lifetime can still affect blocking behavior.

blocks.text: An asynchronous function returns a future immediately, but the caller’s scope still blocks when an unused future is destroyed. Another task returns a future that never becomes ready because its producer was abandoned. The word asynchronous describes a separation in time; it does not specify launch policy, ownership, cancellation, or completion behavior by itself.

blocks.text: This chapter treats futures and promises as a result channel. A producer makes one shared state ready with a value or exception. A consumer observes readiness and retrieves the result according to the future’s ownership rules. Task execution remains a separate design question: who runs the callable, what resources it owns, how it is stopped, and what happens when the caller no longer wants the answer.

topics.title: 19.1.1 Producing Deferred Results
topics.summary: A promise owns the producer side of a shared result state, and its future provides a consumer interface. The producer can satisfy the state with a value or an exception. It should do so exactly once under the interface rules. Destroying an unsatisfied promise makes the corresponding future observe a broken-promise error rather than waiting forever for a producer that no longer exists.

topics.summary: future::get waits for readiness when necessary, returns the stored value, or rethrows the stored exception. blocks.text: Waiting for readiness can be useful when the caller has other work to perform, but a wait timeout does not cancel the producer. The task can continue consuming CPU, holding descriptors, or writing external state after the consumer decides it no longer wishes to wait. Cancellation needs a separate cooperative mechanism and an owner responsible for eventual completion and cleanup.

blocks.text: A timed wait should be interpreted as an observation at that point in time. Ready means the state has a stored outcome. Timeout means it was not ready within the requested wait. Deferred indicates a task whose execution has not been launched under the relevant async policy. Treating all non-ready outcomes as the same event can cause either accidental blocking or abandoned work.

topics.title: 19.2.1 Using std::async
topics.summary: std::async returns a future associated with a callable’s result. With launch::async, it arranges asynchronous execution under the facility’s rules. With launch::deferred, invocation is postponed until a suitable waiting or retrieval operation requests it. The default policy can permit either behavior, so code that requires actual concurrency should not silently rely on the default choosing a new execution path.

blocks.text: std::async combines a callable with a standard-library-managed result state and an execution policy. With an explicit asynchronous policy, it runs the task in the specified asynchronous manner and makes the outcome available through a future. With a deferred policy, execution is postponed until the appropriate wait or retrieval triggers it. An omitted policy permits implementation choices that callers must not silently assume away.

topics.summary: A deferred future can report future_status::deferred to wait_for, while an asynchronously executing task may report timeout or ready. Waiting status is not a performance measurement or a guarantee that the task has made a particular amount of progress. Avoid polling a future in a tight loop when a blocking result wait or event-driven design fits the requirement.
